numerical_failure.affected_api: numba overload of numpy.unique (used by np.union1d) in numba's jitted np.unique implementation; module path not given in passages
numerical_failure.observed_behavior: Inside an @njit function, np.union1d(np.array([np.nan]), np.array([np.nan])) returns a different result than the same call in plain Python; np.unique did not handle np.nan correctly because np.nan == np.nan is False. A later test with np.union1d(np.array([np.nan, 1]), np.array([np.nan])) gave ACTUAL array([ 1., nan]) versus DESIRED array([nan]), shapes (2,) vs (1,) mismatch.
numerical_failure.expected_behavior: The jitted result should match the pure-Python result, e.g. np.union1d(np.array([np.nan]), np.array([np.nan])) should equal [nan] as produced by NumPy; the jitted and Python results should agree (checked with np.testing.assert_equal against expected = union1d_njit.py_func()).
trigger_conditions: call is made inside an @njit (numba jitted) function
np.union1d is called on arrays containing nan, which uses the np.unique overload

input_output_examples.buggy_output: output differs from the Python version (printed output truncated in passage: '[na')

oracle_clues: reference implementation is the non-jitted NumPy call via .py_func()
AssertionError: Arrays are not equal (shapes (2,), (1,) mismatch)

category_specific_evidence: Special values involved: only NaN. The passages do not discuss +/-inf, signed zero, or subnormals.
NaN enters through the np.unique overload in numba/np/arrayobj.py (np_unique_impl), which sorts the flattened input with np.sort and then drops consecutive duplicates by comparing b[i] != x.

Correct handling per the fix: consecutive NaNs are treated as duplicates via not (np.isnan(b[i]) and np.isnan(x)), so np.union1d(np.array([np.nan]), np.array([np.nan])) should yield [nan], matching NumPy.

Reproducer from issue#10069 calls np.union1d inside @njit and compares against the plain Python call; the jitted output is truncated to '[na' in the passage, and the PR discussion reports array([ 1., nan]) versus expected array([nan]) for np.union1d(np.array([np.nan, 1]), np.array([np.nan])).
Oracle clues: np.testing.assert_equal(actual, expected) with expected = union1d_njit.py_func(), giving 'Arrays are not equal (shapes (2,), (1,) mismatch)'.
Regression test added in numba/tests/test_array_methods.py: check(np.array([np.nan, np.nan])).
dtype: the passages never state the dtype of the inputs; np.array([np.nan]) implies a float array but no passage says float64 or that the defect is specific to one dtype, so dtype is null.
Precision and magnitude regimes are not stated in any passage; the tolerance is not stated either, since the oracle uses exact equality via np.testing.assert_equal.
Whether union1d has an independent logic error is unresolved in the passages (PR#10088 discussion).
reproduction_risks: The dtype of the failing inputs is not stated, so a reproduction should use the exact reproducer arrays (np.array([np.nan]) and np.array([np.nan, 1])) rather than assuming a dtype.
The buggy njit output is truncated in the passage ('[na'), so the exact buggy output for the single-NaN case is not confirmed.
The passages do not state where NaNs sort relative to other values, so reproduction should not assume a specific ordering.
The PR notes the solution may not be the most appropriate, and reviewers questioned whether union1d has an independent logic error.

provenance.value: numba overload of numpy.unique (used by np.union1d) in numba's jitted np.unique implementation; module path not given in passages

Inside an @njit function, np.union1d(np.array([np.nan]), np.array([np.nan])) returns a different result than the same call in plain Python; np.unique did not handle np.nan correctly because np.nan == np.nan is False. A later test with np.union1d(np.array([np.nan, 1]), np.array([np.nan])) gave ACTUAL array([ 1., nan]) versus DESIRED array([nan]), shapes (2,) vs (1,) mismatch.

The jitted result should match the pure-Python result, e.g. np.union1d(np.array([np.nan]), np.array([np.nan])) should equal [nan] as produced by NumPy; the jitted and Python results should agree (checked with np.testing.assert_equal against expected = union1d_njit.py_func()).
